CPU and GPU dataframe execution on one H100 host: a prospective blocked comparison of Polars and Spark

Daniel Ejiofor

Complete ten-block recovery analysis, 2026-10-28 UTC. The primary sample contains 400 fresh sessions under one fixed JVM profile. An exploratory pilot, an incomplete lost-host campaign and an aborted default-profile replacement have separate evidential roles; their timings are excluded from primary inference. A separate twenty-wave same-host contention extension is descriptive. Its observations neither replace nor augment the isolated primary sample.

Abstract

We compare Polars CPU, cuDF-Polars GPU, Spark CPU, and GPU-accelerated Spark on one H100 host, including compatible Polars 1.44.2 paths and a same-Python Polars 2.0 CPU control. Six selected queries derived from TPC-H run at five scales; six complex queries run at three scales. A default-profile replacement halted after 88 scientifically validated sessions when Spark CPU reported a Java heap-space error during a first warmup. Its timings are excluded from the fresh recovery sample. A separate feasibility diagnostic returned twelve oracle-valid outputs, and repeated SF1 readiness compared 116 successful outputs before one fresh 400-session recovery cohort began with a fixed Spark JVM allocation-retry profile. The design retains ten paired blocks, independent SQL correctness checks, separate action/common-host-result endpoints, and 26 primary comparisons with Holm adjustment. Strict unsupported expressions receive no imputed times. The profile is a post-incident configuration choice, with no causal mitigation or reliability claim. All 400 recovery sessions completed, with 9,360 oracle-valid outputs. All 26 prespecified tests reject after Holm adjustment: fifteen favor the GPU path and eleven favor its reference. At baseline SF300, CPU/GPU score ratios are 3.296 (pointwise 95% interval 3.239-3.355) for Spark, 3.537 (3.473-3.602) for Polars 1.44.2 CPU/Polars GPU and 2.451 (2.405-2.498) for Polars 2.0 CPU/Polars GPU. GPU Spark does not beat CPU Polars 2.0 on a complete-suite score at any sampled condition: their SF300 ratios are 0.698 (0.687-0.710) for baseline and 0.493 (0.479-0.507) for complex. Descriptive query results nevertheless favor GPU Spark for the window query and selected Q1/Q13 conditions. Strict Polars GPU supports four of six complex expressions and has no complete complex score. No available endpoint comparison changes point-estimate direction when measured through a common host result. A separate twenty-wave contention extension verifies 460 outputs and 110 common measured action pairs; it supplies no primary observations or causal slowdown estimate. These selected research workloads are not complete or certified TPC-H results.

1. Introduction

Dataframe users choosing between a CPU path and a GPU path face two connected questions: whether the selected expressions execute with the intended semantics, and whether a complete supported workload becomes faster at the data sizes they use. A fast subset cannot answer the complete-workload question when the remaining expressions are unsupported. Comparisons also depend on the timing boundary: process startup, materialization and conversion to a common host representation are distinct costs.

We study these questions for Polars CPU, strict cuDF-Polars GPU, Spark CPU and Spark with the RAPIDS plugin on one H100 host. The design compares five fixed software configurations, including two CPU Polars versions, on shared physical inputs. We ask where the prespecified contrasts support a GPU advantage, which unchanged expressions strict Polars GPU can translate, and which operators appear in final Spark plans. These are configuration comparisons; the same host does not isolate a causal effect of GPU hardware alone.

An exploratory H100 pilot motivated the comparisons and current CPU control. Its within-process repeats do not establish process-level replication. The prospective campaign retains the workload and collects fresh sessions in paired blocks, addressing repetition levels, uncertainty and setup bias. Kalibera and Jones, Mytkowicz et al.

The contribution is an auditable empirical comparison with four linked properties: fresh process-level replication in a balanced prospective schedule; independent SQL checks of every successful action; explicit expression coverage without imputed unsupported times; and separate primary action and descriptive common-host-result endpoints. The archive binds each claim to the exact source, inputs, schedule and raw artifacts that produced it. No novelty claim about GPU database architecture is needed for this bounded comparison to be useful.

The scope excludes distributed scaling, equal-cost performance, energy, controlled cold-cache latency and optimal per-engine tuning. Historical A100/H100 comparisons also change CPU allocation, software and file layout. Primary recovery conclusions apply to the explicitly recorded JVM profile; the aborted cohorts do not estimate its causal performance or reliability effect. The user-requested contention extension asks a different question about two coordinated workloads sharing the same host. It has separate sampling, instrumentation and descriptive reporting, and supplies no extra primary blocks.

2. Related work and methodological position

Systems benchmark repetition occurs at several levels. Kalibera and Jones distinguish variation between builds, executions and inner iterations, and argue that replication should address the level contributing uncertainty. Our inner actions summarize one fresh session; ten paired blocks supply the observations used for inference. We do not treat thirty inner actions as thirty independent sessions or claim that ten blocks guarantee a desired precision. Kalibera and Jones

Experimental layout can change measured conclusions even when the setup appears innocuous. Mytkowicz and colleagues demonstrate this problem and motivate setup randomization. Blocking provides a complementary way to organize comparisons around nuisance variation. Here, shared block/condition identities, randomized condition order and balanced configuration orders address allocation; they do not demonstrate constant host conditions or independence. Mytkowicz et al., NIST

The study fixes one family of 26 primary comparisons before observing their results and applies Holm adjustment. Query-level and endpoint sensitivity analyses have a different, descriptive role. The t intervals on block log ratios remain model dependent; resampling the same ten observations would not create further independent evidence. Hesterberg’s discussion of small-sample bootstrap undercoverage is a reason to state these limits, rather than to present bootstrap computation as a replacement for replication. Holm, Hesterberg

Implementation documentation supplies a different kind of evidence. Polars GPU support, Spark AQE and the pinned RAPIDS compatibility notes explain why strict guards, final plans and explicit semantic rules are required. They cannot establish that a particular measured action used the intended path or returned a valid result; the saved session artifacts provide those checks. Likewise, TPC-H supplies workload provenance, while this selected-query, fixed-parameter Float64 experiment has a narrower identity than the complete standard benchmark. Polars, Spark 3.5.9, RAPIDS 26.08.1, TPC-H 3.0.1

The recovery profile has a limited technical rationale. The OpenJDK allocation- starvation issue discusses GCLocker retries and possible longer stalls; it does not diagnose this study’s failure. JEP 423 changes G1 JNI critical-region handling in JDK 22, while this experiment retains Java 17.0.20.1. The Spark proposal that used retry count 100 was closed unmerged, so it is not official Spark 3.5.9 tuning guidance. These sources motivate a separately gated feasibility diagnostic, not a claimed cure or measured causal benefit. OpenJDK JDK-8192647, JEP 423, Spark PR 51920

3. Materials and implementations

3.1 Host and software

The replacement Linux KVM host exposes one H100 80 GB HBM3 GPU, 26 Xeon Platinum 8480+ vCPUs and 237,490,843,648 RAM bytes, approximately 221 GiB. Its driver is 580.105.08 and kernel is 6.8.0-1046-nvidia. Archived readiness inventory records OpenJDK 17.0.20.1, CUDA driver API 13.0 and CUDA runtime 12.9. The CUDA 12 package closure is pinned; the driver’s advertised compatibility level does not change the runtime version used by these environments. The lost host used driver 570.148.08 and a different kernel; its incomplete campaign cannot establish the replacement host’s performance.

The frozen replacement inventories verify the same CPython 3.11.13 base executable/build (Clang 20.1.4) and matching common non-GPU package pins in both environments. GPU dependencies differ because the selected cuDF-Polars release requires older Polars. The historical CPU control used Python 3.10.12 and remains separate.

Spark retains the a100-parity settings, including a 96 GiB driver heap, 120 shuffle partitions, adaptive query execution, and UTC session time zone. GPU Spark uses two concurrent GPU tasks and a 2 GiB pinned-memory pool. The plan archives these settings and the plugin JAR SHA256; the complete audit verifies their effective values in every final session. Polars uses the allocated 26-thread setting without an equivalent fixed host-memory limit. Consequently, common hardware does not imply equal memory budgets. Spark AQE can change joins and partitioning using runtime statistics; final plans are retained for interpretation. Spark 3.5.9 documentation

The recovery applies the following sealed driver startup profile to both Spark configurations at every suite/scale:

SPARK_SUBMIT_OPTS=-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:GCLockerRetryAllocationCount=100 -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal

Java 17.0.20.1, G1, the 96 GiB maximum heap and all listed query settings remain fixed. PrintFlagsFinal records the effective driver options before query timing. Competing Java-option variables must be absent; the profile must not be injected through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, which also affects Spark’s command builder. EXECUTION_PROFILE.json binds the exact startup environment, Java executable/runtime files, launcher sources, Python environments and diagnostic/input/oracle evidence before recovery timing. Its exact SHA256 and pre-start identity are recorded in §4.1. The four repeated Spark readiness driver logs verify the profile, as do all 160 formal Spark driver logs and 24 idle-boundary profile receipts in the complete audit. Allocation-retry and GC stalls within an action remain inside its normal endpoints; no such observation is excluded as an outlier.

Polars GPU sets raise_on_fail=True, verifies the effective configuration, runs a positive GPU canary, and requires an unsupported CPU-only canary to raise. The streaming policy fallback_mode=warn concerns a possible fallback to a single GPU partition in the installed release; it does not authorize CPU translation fallback. Spark GPU may retain CPU operators. Installed source and guards define behavior; rolling documentation is contextual. Polars GPU support, pinned Spark plugin compatibility

DuckDB 1.5.6’s tpch extension generated the inputs, exported as Snappy Parquet under the archived recipe. Configurations share files and fixed manifests; full SHA256 checks run before/after the campaign outside measurements. Nominal scale factors are generator settings. The default-profile replacement inputs were freshly generated using the pinned recipe. Their manifest and physical file identities remain the inputs for the recovery, which reuses the same 1,654 files and existing independent oracle bytes on the same VM. No recovery input regeneration or mutation is allowed. No claim of physical-byte identity with the lost instance is made. The archived replacement inventory is therefore also the recovery inventory below; the recorded pre/post full-byte gates verify those bytes. Generation uses 30 export threads, a 64 GB memory setting, Snappy compression, 122,880-row groups, per-thread output and a 128 MB target file size. 4. Prospective experimental design

4.1 Campaign identity, allocation and replication

The frozen experimental source is code commit c84ef6a07341f350dae6636ab709c1b65fd894e0, comprising a 52-file source snapshot. Four cohorts have distinct evidential roles. The exploratory pilot supplies motivation and historical observations. The October 26 prospective campaign was created at 2026-10-26 18:11:05 UTC with campaign SHA256 69669dfbc74ffb2a0c378c319c7b886043ffccb8f301784fb2b73b9ab32581e0; its host was lost before completion. Only three complete core checkpoints, 120 sessions and 2,808 successful output comparisons survive. It lacks final input-byte verification and a complete raw telemetry archive, and contributes no timings to either later primary sample.

The October 27 default-profile replacement used the same frozen source, design, seed, queries, settings and inferential method. Its campaign ID is h100-confirmatory-replacement-20261027, with campaign SHA256 0dabe0d40c5adda0a087508e3f95ceb0636815f5133a3b401071612e3f24c145 and pre-start manifest SHA256 a758ceea7d16a6c726221db5db2cb99502ac4f640131341b456e9b63ed459b2a. All 358 files in the pre-start archive were preserved off-host and verified; private Git commit b94372deebcf3503c115fd9cc396dec3666ce85b preceded the first confirmatory action. This archive includes fresh runtime inventories, all five input manifests, ten SF1 readiness sessions with 116 successful SQL output comparisons, five semantic fixture runs, and all eight independent full-scale oracle outputs. Readiness and oracle execution are outside the confirmatory performance sample. That cohort subsequently halted at 20:27:48 UTC with 88 scientifically validated sessions, 2,056 successful output comparisons and one failed session. Its remaining 311 sessions had not started. The complete abort and evidence disposition are reported in §5.1. No default-profile timing is carried into recovery inference, and its journal/attempts remain unchanged.

The fourth cohort, h100-confirmatory-gclocker100-20261027, began collection on October 27 at 21:47:44 UTC. Its canonical archive is evidence-research/20261027/h100-confirmatory-gclocker100-v1. The registered campaign SHA256 is 3142874b918a2df2d66c8dfb32c26f59a09353edcb4cb73e51c4ba46ff387641; the pre-start manifest SHA256 is ea57fa1221b905e8ee287fe7860285c7a37535b084f13ce3dbbbca5ac4e29ace; the sealed execution-profile SHA256 is a07569ffa3be9cd138ed63084ff59ed668b8bceeef355b5a4f63adef53464c69. The canonical pre-start snapshot contains 346 files, including its manifest; all 345 listed file checksums match. Private commit 6dbca2fbd4de1be8aa4408a639954bc9076bfa38 preceded the first session. The recorded full 1,654-file initial byte gate passed at 21:47:43.892782 UTC. The final full-byte gate passed at 2026-10-28 23:33:18.564788 UTC, after the last session ended. All 1,654 files retain their recorded identities.

Exactly one separately named full-complex-SF100 Spark CPU feasibility session completed before recovery preparation. It used seed 838471203, one warmup and one measured action per query. Its validation completed at 21:36:41.579958 UTC with all twelve oracle-valid records, twelve checked cleanup records, successful process exit and the five effective driver flags. The archive preserves diagnostic-sf100-driver_log.log, diagnostic-sf100-results.json and diagnostic-sf100-validation.json, with hashes bound by the sealed profile. Its timings are excluded from primary inference. This passed feasibility test does not establish mitigation efficacy or guaranteed robustness.

All five configurations then repeated SF1 readiness. The readiness report completed at 21:44:41.187289 UTC with ten smoke sessions, 116 successful SQL output comparisons, five semantic fixture configurations and no errors. All four Spark readiness driver logs show retry count 100, G1, unlocked diagnostics, PrintFlagsFinal and maximum heap 103,079,215,104 bytes. Passing before/after readiness profile receipts bind the same sealed profile. These pre-start observations are excluded from the confirmatory performance sample.

The recovery retains the same VM, 1,654 physical files, existing oracle bytes, five configurations and unchanged 52-file C84 source. The fixed Spark JVM profile is an explicitly disclosed post-incident change. All ten blocks and 400 single-attempt sessions completed; the final replay binds the same profile and excludes every earlier timing cohort.

The design is ten blocks by eight suite/scale conditions by five configurations, yielding 400 fresh sessions. Each supported query has one recorded warmup, excluded from performance estimates, and three measured actions in a session. A fresh Python process or Spark JVM prevents reuse of the previous configuration’s engine session, application table cache, or allocator. The three actions define a session median; they do not increase the independent inferential sample size beyond ten paired blocks.

For each condition, the ten sequences of an odd-five Williams design balance each configuration across positions and each ordered predecessor pair. The base sequence is [0,1,4,2,3]; cyclic relabelings and reversals supply the ten orders. Seed 20261026 fixes relabeling and sequence allocation. Condition order is randomized separately in each block. The five configurations within a block/condition share a recorded measured-query shuffle seed; warmup query order is fixed. Blocking and randomization reduce nuisance effects but do not prove independence or remove all temporal drift. NIST randomized-block guidance

The recovery requires all ten fresh blocks and all 400 fresh sessions. Ten blocks is a fixed allocation, not a power guarantee. No earlier timing enters that allocation, and there is no significance-based stopping, trimming, selective repetition or tuning. Unexpected errors halt execution; retained attempts and partial outputs support explicit deviation assessment. A recovery failure does not authorize automatic parameter escalation, restart or another cohort until a clean result appears.

4.2 Timing boundaries and host state

The primary seconds endpoint starts before query construction and ends after materialized collect(). It includes optimization, Parquet reading, execution, and result collection, while excluding process/session setup, table setup, plan serialization, sampler shutdown, and cleanup. Polars returns a host DataFrame; Spark returns Python Rows. The endpoint retains this API conversion asymmetry for continuity with the pilot.

Secondary host_result_seconds continues from the same start through Python dictionary conversion in both paths, excluding normalization/serialization. Endpoint direction changes are reported in §5.5. Startup, process wall time and action bounds are separate. A sum of six query medians is a suite score, not observed once-through latency.

All Parquet files at the selected scale are read before each session. Linux mincore snapshots are recorded immediately before/after this preheat and after the worker exits, together with memory, swap, faults, and disk counters. A residency snapshot cannot guarantee that pages remain resident during execution. The policy is attempted filesystem preheating with observed residency, not a controlled cold-cache or guaranteed in-memory benchmark. Application DataFrame caching is disabled.

Baseline has no explicit cleanup barrier; complex uses verified Python/JVM GC and active-job/shuffle checks outside action timers. Cleanup remains in process wall time. Sequential execution, exclusivity checks and process-group cleanup support control without establishing dedicated hardware or constant clocks. Plans show operator selection, not kernel/transfer times or runtime fractions. Additional profiling must remain outside primary timings.

Read-only status probes remain part of the instrumented virtual host. The replacement operational supervisor pauses after each complete 40-session block and snapshots all block raw files, including logs, telemetry, events, plans, outputs and scientific gates. The next block requires an off-host receipt tied to the exact campaign and snapshot hashes. Transfers occur while no engine session is running. Backup pauses and receipt times are retained as an operational pacing amendment; they add no sessions and change no expressions, action boundaries or scheduled order. Full input-byte hashing, oracle execution and tests on the benchmark host remain outside engine measurements.

A separate local power event delayed the block06 off-host handoff on October 28. The controlling Mac’s selected power records show Low Power Sleep at 09:13:38 UTC on 1% battery and wake on AC attachment at 14:11:23 UTC. Local watcher observations bracket the gap at 09:13:25.168866 and 14:11:52.581715 UTC. Meanwhile, the remote block06 final session succeeded at 11:15:26.689677 UTC; its backup control was created at 11:15:30.821446 UTC and acknowledged off-host at 14:12:51.939753 UTC, 10,641.118307 s later. The existing controller and sleep-prevention process survived, and the remote supervisor continued the original schedule into block07 after the receipt, without restart or replacement. This local control/backup delay is distinct from the managed contention hold in §4.6 and supplies no GPU/JVM failure diagnosis. No action, worker or outer-wall timestamp is corrected. The longer between-block interval remains part of the host’s temporal/cache history; no performance effect is inferred from it.

The recovery retains 24 idle-boundary execution-profile receipts: before/after repeated readiness, before/after each of ten blocks, and before/ after final verification. The final complete audit binds those receipts to the sealed profile, unchanged Java/Python environments, session bounds and campaign completion. These new receipts are configuration checks, not extra timing observations.

4.3 Correctness and coverage

Before default-profile replacement timing, DuckDB 1.5.6 executed the original SQL definitions for all eight measured conditions using the same Float64 normalization. The recovery reuses those frozen complete oracle bytes. Each oracle contains complete ordered rows, SQL/source/manifest hashes, and effective resource settings. Its execution is outside competitor performance scores. This provides an independent execution engine for the specified SQL, not an independent proof that the SQL specification is correct.

Every successful warmup and measured result must match its frozen oracle: column sets, row counts, and ordered rows; exact nulls, strings, dates, and integer pairs; finite floating values within relative tolerance 1e-8 or absolute tolerance 1e-6. The audit retains numeric discrepancies. Parallel floating reductions may differ in operation order, so tolerance-based agreement does not imply bitwise identity or exact decimal arithmetic.

Strict Polars GPU rejection of the original Q13 DOTALL-regex expression and grouped-window expression remains explicit. Rejections have no imputed time. A complete suite score requires all six queries and all three measured actions to succeed and pass the oracle. Four supported complex queries cannot supply a six-query Polars GPU score. Coverage is part of the result.

Five separate hand-checked semantic cases cover duplicate/null join keys, outer counts, a nonempty semi/anti exclusion, rank ties/nulls, and multiline regex/distinct behavior. Their corrected diagnostic plans do not replace any performance query. A regression preserves a null-ordering mismatch observed in the original Polars 1.44.2 window port: with prices 100, 100, null, 50, its top-three keys are 3, 1, 2 instead of SQL’s 1, 2, 4. The earlier cohort’s full-scale input-domain checks find no null price/date/order/customer keys in the generated orders table at all five scales. The default-profile replacement repeated these SQL counts against all five fresh inputs before confirmation and likewise found zero nulls in those fields. Original-port claims are bounded to the archived tested domain; the adversarial limitation remains disclosed.

4.4 Estimands, uncertainty, and multiplicity

For block b, configuration e, and query q, let m[b,e,q] be the median of the three measured primary action times. A complete-suite score is S[b,e] = sum_q m[b,e,q]. For a prespecified reference/GPU comparison, L[b] = log(S[b,reference] / S[b,GPU]). The reported speedup estimate is exp(mean_b L[b]). Thus it is the geometric mean of paired block score ratios, rather than a ratio of pooled times or an arithmetic mean speedup. Ratios above one favor the denominator GPU configuration.

Two-sided pointwise 95% intervals are obtained by exponentiating mean(L) ± t(0.975,9) × sd(L)/sqrt(10). The corresponding two-sided tests evaluate mean log ratio zero. The model assumes independent, approximately normal block log ratios. Raw ratios, order and spread support assessment. Ten blocks may leave wide uncertainty; zero observed variance cannot prove reproducibility. Inner actions or resamples add no independent observations; small-sample bootstrapping is not an automatic remedy. Hesterberg

Primary comparison, numerator / denominator Conditions Tests
CPU Polars 2.0 / GPU Spark All eight suite/scale conditions 8
CPU Spark / GPU Spark All eight suite/scale conditions 8
CPU Polars 1.44.2 / Polars GPU Five baseline scales 5
CPU Polars 2.0 / Polars GPU Five baseline scales 5

The 26-test family uses Holm adjustment at familywise alpha 0.05. A supported GPU advantage requires an estimated ratio above one and adjusted p < 0.05, conditional on the model assumptions. Pointwise intervals are not simultaneous intervals. Lack of a supported difference does not establish equivalence. Failed/incomplete comparisons remain explicit and do not silently shrink the family. Query-level and host-result estimates are descriptive secondary results, with pointwise intervals and no added primary claims. Holm

Crossover statements identify only sampled scale points. The protocol’s supported-bracket rule requires a supported advantage at the upper measured point without a contradictory larger sampled point. A lower point lacking support is not evidence of reversal. No exact byte threshold or interpolation through unmeasured scales is asserted.

4.5 Separate coordinated same-host contention experiment

The owner subsequently requested concurrent sessions on the existing H100. The separate contention protocol defines h100-contention-20261028, with canonical pre-start archive evidence-research/20261028/h100-contention-v1. Its plan SHA256 is 670f37af6c1a6f2dbea5fc110d213b148a0acb83858786a21add8252acc89031 and pre-start manifest SHA256 is 4088b5302a7d42c8aa87ebaed06e229bed3b0783bd15cf6556a6110981bf9f25. All 65 listed file checksums match, for 66 canonical files including the manifest. Private pre-start commit 98c7ff4d6a9bbe82a021671c28fed28f71827b70 preceded execution. The plan binds the recovery campaign/profile identities above, the same 52-file C84 source, SF30/SF100 manifests, four existing independent oracles and separately versioned external instrumentation. No contention observation enters the isolated 400-session sample, its 26-test family or the recovery feasibility diagnostic.

Pair Concurrent participants GPU path
A Spark GPU and Polars CPU 2.0.0 Spark GPU
B Spark CPU and strict Polars GPU 1.44.2 Polars GPU

Each pair has one Spark JVM with its original 96 GiB heap and one GPU execution path. Each participant requests its full original 26 CPU threads on the same 26-vCPU host; CPUs are not partitioned into disjoint allocations or cgroups. Both Spark paths retain the sealed retry-100 JVM profile and fixed SQL settings. Host memory, CPU, cache, disk and GPU-related host work are deliberately shared. The design excludes two concurrent Spark heaps and simultaneous Spark GPU/ Polars GPU default pools. These observations cannot describe equal-resource competition or standalone isolated execution.

The staged pilot contains both pairs × baseline/complex at SF30: four waves and eight fresh processes, with one warmup and one measured action per query. Seed 20261028 fixes its wave order. Only if all four pilot waves pass output, cleanup, configuration and actual measured-overlap gates may the planned expansion run: both pairs × both suites × SF30/SF100 × two repetitions, sixteen waves and thirty-two fresh processes, with order seed 20261029. Pilot observations are not pooled into the expansion. Expected successful output comparisons are 92 for the pilot and 368 for the expansion, with two and eight expected strict unsupported warmups respectively. These are the prespecified coverage counts; actual audit accounting is reported in §5.7. Any failed wave stops its phase and preserves both participants and partial evidence. The design permits no hidden retry, adaptive sample increase or new scale; a failure requires a new explicit scientific decision.

The separately hashed contention_worker.py imports the byte-identical frozen worker. External hooks add an engine-ready barrier and a rendezvous before each common query/phase/trial. The action rendezvous follows the first existing process-counter sample and precedes the original timer start; both participants use the same future monotonic release timestamp. Query expressions, materialization/conversion code and timer statements remain unchanged. This is coordinated same-query contention, rather than independent arrival traffic. Each wave shares one full selected-scale preheat before either process starts, with residency observations before/after preheat and after both workers. Selected input-byte gates bracket each phase; these observations do not guarantee in-query residency.

In pair B complex, strict Polars GPU rejects cx_q13 and cx_window during warmup. Both warmup attempts rendezvous, but their measured CPU counterparts explicitly bypass the barrier because no measured GPU counterpart exists. Those two CPU measurements are unpaired diagnostics. A six-query CPU sum would mix paired and unpaired conditions and must not be presented as uniformly contended execution; a complete six-query Polars GPU score remains unavailable. Only the four common measured query pairs establish query-level contention for this condition. Other waves require six common measured query pairs.

Saved action UTC and same-host monotonic intervals, rather than overlapping process lifetimes, must establish actual action overlap. Report both action durations, start skew and interval intersection for every common measured query; the pilot gate requires positive intersection on both clocks. The action and common-host-result endpoints retain their frozen boundaries. Wave/process wall time includes initialization and rendezvous waits, with shared preheat reported separately. Process-counter deltas and sampled RSS/GPU-memory observations can include untimed rendezvous waits and are not isolated action-only resource costs. Separate wave telemetry samples host/process trees every 0.5 s and the GPU board every 200 ms; the worker samplers retain their separately recorded intervals. Transient peaks may be missed, and board utilization/power cannot be attributed causally to a single query or process.

No contention p values, superiority decisions, additions to the primary family or exact crossover thresholds are declared. Two expansion repetitions support descriptive reporting only. Any later comparison with the completed isolated study must disclose the different replication, barrier and preheat context and keep both designs’ observations separate.

4.6 Managed interlude in isolated collection

The interlude record discloses a requested operational amendment after isolated collection began. The manager held only the exact isolated scheduler, PID 179144, at 2026-10-28 04:44:23 UTC, preserving its process, locks and journal. The already launched isolated SF30 Spark CPU runner and its workers continued unpaused. ORIGINAL_RUNNER_DRAINED.json records runner exit zero and schedule/result hashes at 04:45:43.946178 UTC, before the pilot start at 04:47:43 UTC. The frozen original action/host-result timer code is unchanged. The terminal offline audit now binds all 34 original block-04-complex-sf30-spark_cpu/attempt-001 files from the protected off-host block04 backup. It checks 33 immutable payload files byte for byte and binds session.json to its frozen identity while allowing only documented parent finalization; the later SCIENTIFIC_VALIDATION.json is retained separately. Its original result and schedule hashes match the drain receipt. The last original host-result endpoint is 04:45:38.505969 UTC; the first contention action starts at 04:47:59.693693 UTC, 141.188 s later. Saved action endpoints therefore establish temporal separation independently of the operational drain receipt.

Because the scheduler is held while its existing child drains, the journal may continue to mark the attempt as running after its worker has finished. The scheduler’s ended_at_utc and orchestrator_wall_seconds include the hold. The retained attempt reports an outer wall of 3,043.015 s and an end timestamp of 05:32:20.060856 UTC, while its Spark worker process wall is 240.581 s, ending at 04:45:41.907405 UTC. The outer envelope includes the scheduler hold and must not be interpreted as worker or query latency. These original values are preserved. The hold does not create a replacement attempt or cancel the remaining 400-session allocation.

The saved handoff records the same scheduler PID 179144, creation time 1793160829.75, resumed at 05:32:20.044724 UTC. STATE.json is COMPLETE_RESUMED; the phase driver is COMPLETE_OFFHOST, both phase raw backups are verified off-host, and the owned-group cleanup receipt lists no live members. PROFILE_BEFORE_RESUME.json records PASS at 05:32:19.993450 UTC. These interlude checks are separate receipts and do not replace or augment the formal 24-record profile log. The original unchanged schedule continues. The last contention host-result endpoint is 05:28:37.930202 UTC, before this resume. The terminal handoff audit reports PASS, verifies the original payload and action separation, and records no unresolved reasons. Temporal separation does not remove the interlude’s change to pacing or demonstrate unchanged host/cache conditions; possible carryover remains a limitation.

5. Results

All primary estimates below come from the complete fresh recovery cohort. The genuine portable replay is PASS, phase complete and nonsynthetic; no pilot, lost-host, aborted replacement, readiness, diagnostic or contention timing enters its ten-block estimates. The primary tables retain all prespecified contrasts, including supported reference advantages.

5.1 Cohort disposition and completed recovery

The default-profile replacement halted at 20:27:48 UTC on October 27. Its failed session, block-03-complex-sf100-spark_cpu, failed in cx_q09’s first warmup, before any successful output or measured observation in that session. The JVM exited 52 and reported java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space, preceded by GCLocker allocation-retry warnings. The event-log BlockManager maximum on-heap value, 61,658,785,382 bytes, corroborates the configured 96 GiB heap cap. The nearest host sample recorded 211,723,608,064 available RAM bytes, zero swap use and 2,713,801,965,568 free disk bytes.

These observations do not reveal failure-time heap occupancy or RSS and do not distinguish genuine heap exhaustion from premature allocation failure. No failure-time heap/RSS or GC-recovery evidence was retained, so a root cause and a causal effect of increasing the retry count remain undetermined. Host available memory alone cannot establish whether this JVM could satisfy its particular allocation.

The aborted cohort retains 88 scientifically validated sessions and 2,056 successful output comparisons, one failed session and 311 unstarted sessions. Its complete 3,349-file incident evidence was preserved off-host as a 220,656,964-byte gzip archive with SHA256 79c99819d272cc1af947d8e200976a940cd63a96be580112e4a6c5900adee6ff. Both complete blocks also retain separate verified off-host raw backups. The original journal and attempts were not edited; no successful session was rerun within that cohort, and its failed attempt remains visible. This is a reported failure observation, not a complete primary comparison.

The separate feasibility/readiness results in §4.1 preceded the fresh recovery sample. Its 400 sessions all completed in one successful attempt each, with no replacement observations. Recorded attempt bounds are 2026-10-27 21:47:44.042050 UTC through 2026-10-28 23:26:10.952925 UTC. The final full-input hash gate passed at 23:33:18.564788 UTC and journal completion was recorded at 23:33:18.565015 UTC. The original supervisor exited zero, with its end marker at 23:42:11 UTC. All ten 40-session block backups and final/completion snapshots were verified off-host. The separate managed contention hold and local-power handoff delay are retained as operational pacing disclosures, not removed from saved timestamps.

The independently replayed complete audit reports PASS with no findings. It verifies 400 session identities, 9,360 successful SQL comparisons, 60 specific strict translation rejections, 3,360 successful complex cleanup records and 60 failed-action cleanup records. All 160 formal Spark driver logs prove the sealed retry-100/G1/96 GiB profile, and all 24 ordered idle-boundary receipts match the registered Java/runtime/environment identities. This is successful execution under the chosen profile, not a causal before/after mitigation study.

5.4 Sampled-scale brackets and descriptive query heterogeneity

For baseline Spark CPU/GPU and both baseline CPU Polars/Polars GPU comparisons, SF1 favors the CPU reference and SF10 favors the GPU, with no contradictory larger sampled point. The supported sampled-scale bracket is therefore SF1 to SF10 for each of these three declared comparisons. It does not identify an exact intermediate threshold. GPU Spark never crosses CPU Polars 2.0 on the sampled complete-suite conditions. The complex Spark CPU/GPU comparison already favors the GPU at its smallest measured scale, SF30; no lower crossover bracket is observed. The complex Spark CPU/GPU ratio falls from 3.975933 at SF30 to 2.605614 at SF300, so the gain is not monotone increasing with input scale.

Complete-suite results do not apply uniformly to individual queries. GPU Spark has a shorter descriptive query estimate than CPU Polars 2.0 for baseline Q1 at SF30/SF100/SF300, complex window at all three measured scales, and complex Q13 at SF100/SF300. For example, at SF300 the CPU Polars 2.0/GPU Spark ratio is 5.145 for window but 0.149 for Q9. Table 3 shows all SF300 expressions; the heatmap retains all measured scales. These are geometric means of paired query ratios, without query-level significance tests or additional primary claims. The four supported complex Polars GPU expressions cannot establish a complete six-query score.

Appendix C displays all 260 primary block ratios in chronological block order, without trimming or selective repetition. For every contrast the ten observed ratios are on the same side of one. 6. Discussion

The complete-suite and query-level answers differ. Under these fixed settings, GPU Spark reduces the complete-suite score relative to CPU Spark beyond baseline SF1 and throughout the sampled complex workload. It does not reduce the complete-suite score relative to CPU Polars 2.0 at any sampled condition. Nevertheless, its window-query estimates and selected Q1/Q13 estimates are shorter than CPU Polars 2.0. The workload mix therefore matters: a suite-level CPU preference does not imply that every selected operator favors the CPU. These observations identify useful conditions for further profiling without attributing the result to a particular GPU kernel, transfer path or runtime fraction that was not measured.

Strict Polars GPU provides the supported baseline gains from SF10 onward, including a 2.451-fold CPU Polars 2.0/GPU score ratio at SF300. Its unsupported Q13/window expressions limit the complex result more strongly than its fast supported queries can resolve. Users requiring the unchanged full complex workload cannot substitute the four-query GPU subset. GPU Spark supplies complete execution for that workload, while CPU Polars 2.0 has the lower complete-suite score in this experiment.

The two CPU Polars controls answer different configuration questions. CPU 1.44.2 aligns the frontend with the selected GPU integration; CPU 2.0.0 supplies a newer same-Python control. The SF300 baseline ratio is 3.537 against the former and 2.451 against the latter. These are comparisons of recorded software paths and dependencies, not an isolated causal estimate of a frontend-version change. Likewise, Spark and Polars differ in memory policies, execution APIs and dependency inventories. Common hardware does not turn these comparisons into GPU-hardware-only effects or estimates of globally optimal tuning.

Both endpoints retain the same direction for all available complete-suite pairs. This narrows the endpoint concern for these saved output shapes; it does not justify treating action time as application latency. Neither endpoint includes process startup. A sum of query medians is a defined score, not the elapsed time of an application running a complete suite once. The pointwise intervals express ten-block log-ratio uncertainty, while Holm decisions address the one declared family. The small p values do not expand generalization beyond this host, workload and profile.

The cohort history is part of the result. The replacement host changes driver, kernel and physical file generation relative to the lost host; the later recovery reuses replacement inputs while changing the Spark allocation-retry profile after a failure. The completed fresh sample avoids pooling incompatible timings but does not remove configuration-selection history. The passed feasibility diagnostic and successful recovery do not prove a false OOM, a GCLocker root cause, a cure or a causal reliability gain. Allocation-retry and GC time inside measured actions remains part of the normal endpoints.

The separate contention extension describes synchronized pairs requesting the original full CPU budget on one shared host. Its query observations do not rank GPU engines because the competitors differ. Pair B complex also retains two unpaired CPU diagnostics. No matched isolated-versus-contention slowdown analysis is claimed. Verified action separation and scheduler resume do not establish unchanged cache/host conditions; the managed hold and local-power handoff delay remain visible temporal changes in the primary collection.

7. Validity and interpretation limits

One virtual host, possible temporal dependence, VM interference and ten blocks limit generalization and t-model precision. Williams balance does not eliminate all carryover. Fixed settings, unequal memory policies and differing dependency inventories constrain causal software comparisons. Selected queries, Float64 semantics and the preserved window-domain limitation constrain workload and semantic generalization. Unsupported cases have no imputed speed. Mechanistic explanations involving transfers, compute, spilling or bandwidth require separate runtime evidence. The recovery profile was chosen after an observed failure, limiting inference to that post-incident configuration. A fresh complete sample avoids pooling incompatible timings; it does not erase the configuration-selection history or establish a causal mitigation effect. The fixed single-recovery decision and its completed disposition remain part of the interpretation scope. The same-host contention extension is small and synchronized, with only two planned expansion repetitions. Its process-counter and memory observations may span untimed waits; GPU board samples are shared and can miss peaks. The requested interlude changes isolated temporal pacing and may influence later host/cache state. Recorded idle/identity checks and continued preheat policy support interpretation without proving absence of carryover. The separately recorded local low-power event also delayed a between-block off-host receipt while remote block06 completed. Its added temporal spacing may affect later host/cache conditions, without establishing a measured effect or changing any action/worker timing value.

9. Conclusion

A complete ten-block, 400-session comparison on the recorded H100 host supports GPU gains for specific configuration pairs and scales. GPU Spark beats CPU Spark from baseline SF10 onward and at all three complex scales, but CPU Polars 2.0 has the lower complete-suite score at every sampled condition. GPU Spark still has shorter descriptive estimates for the window query and selected Q1/Q13 conditions. Strict Polars GPU beats both CPU Polars versions on the baseline suite from SF10 onward, while its two unsupported complex expressions prevent any complete complex-suite score.

All 26 prespecified tests reject after Holm adjustment, with fifteen GPU-favoring and eleven reference-favoring directions. Available common-host- result comparisons preserve direction. These findings apply to the fixed post-incident JVM profile, tested input domain and recorded host/pacing history; they establish no general GPU-hardware effect, exact unmeasured crossover, causal mitigation or contention slowdown. The separately completed contention extension remains descriptive and excluded from primary inference.

References

These references support methodological or implementation context. Experimental facts and numerical findings require the separately archived study evidence ledger. Documentation was consulted on 2026-10-26; the related-work synthesis rechecked the primary Kent repository, IBM publication record, NIST handbook and Hesterberg preprint abstract on 2026-10-27. Installed pinned source and recorded effective settings govern runtime claims where rolling documentation differs.

  1. Kalibera, T., and Jones, R. E. (2013). Rigorous Benchmarking in Reasonable Time. Proceedings of ISMM, 63-74. DOI; author manuscript, University of Kent. Supports separating repetition levels, reporting uncertainty, and allocating replication according to variation and experiment cost. It does not establish a universal repetition count or prove that this campaign’s ten blocks have adequate power.

  2. Mytkowicz, T., Diwan, A., Hauswirth, M., and Sweeney, P. F. (2009). Producing Wrong Data Without Doing Anything Obviously Wrong! Proceedings of ASPLOS. Primary publication record, IBM Research. Supports caution about setup bias and experimental allocation. It does not demonstrate the absence of bias on this virtual host.

  3. NIST/SEMATECH. e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, section 5.3.3.2, Randomized Block Designs. Official handbook. Supplies general blocking/randomization principles. The exact Williams sequences and balance checks are part of this study’s frozen protocol and executable schedule tests.

  4. Holm, S. (1979). A Simple Sequentially Rejective Multiple Test Procedure. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics, 6(2), 65-70. Publisher archive record. Source of the familywise multiple-testing procedure applied to the single prespecified 26-test family. This does not make the reported pointwise confidence intervals simultaneous or remove the assumptions behind input p values.

  5. Hesterberg, T. C. (2015). What Teachers Should Know About the Bootstrap: Resampling in the Undergraduate Statistics Curriculum. The American Statistician, 69(4), 371-386. DOI; author preprint. Motivates caution about small-sample bootstrap coverage and the distinction between original observations and computational resamples. The manuscript’s log-ratio t model remains an assumption-dependent prespecified choice.

  6. Transaction Processing Performance Council. TPC Benchmark H Standard Specification, revision 3.0.1. Official specification. Defines the complete query/refresh workload, standard timing and metrics. This selected-query Float64 study does not claim those metrics, compliance or certification. Notice and provenance records are retained separately in the private research archive.

  7. DuckDB. Version 1.5 documentation, tpch extension. Official documentation; tagged 1.5.6 SQL query source. Documents generator use, deviations from official generated data and fixed substitution parameters. Generator/version provenance does not establish benchmark compliance.

  8. Polars. GPU Support, user guide. Official documentation. Describes GPU collection and raise_on_fail=True. This study additionally saves effective configuration and positive/unsupported session canaries; documentation alone does not prove execution mode.

  9. Apache Spark. Spark 3.5.9 SQL Performance Tuning. Official versioned documentation. Describes AQE, caching, partition and join configuration, supporting retention of actual settings and final plans. It is not a prescription that the chosen fixed settings are optimal for every engine.

  10. NVIDIA. cuDF plugin for Apache Spark, version 26.08.1 compatibility. Pinned official source. Documents ordering and floating-point differences relevant to comparison semantics. Exact result checks and selected operators still require saved study artifacts.

  11. NVIDIA. cuDF-Polars profiling and tracing. Official versioned documentation. Distinguishes runtime profiling from plan interpretation. The current manuscript makes no kernel-time, transfer-time, or GPU-runtime-fraction claim. APIs must be checked against installed 26.10.2 before any additional diagnostic run.

  12. OpenJDK. JDK-8192647, GCLocker allocation issue record. Primary issue tracker. The prospective recovery protocol cites this record for allocation-starvation behavior and discussion of retry count as a possible workaround with longer-stall risk. It supplies a plausible mechanism, not a diagnosis of this study’s Java heap-space error, proof of a false OOM or a causal mitigation result.

  13. OpenJDK. JEP 423. Official JEP. Addresses G1 JNI critical-region handling in JDK 22. The recovery retains Java 17.0.20.1; citing this JEP does not imply that its implementation is present in the study runtime or that the study upgrades Java.

  14. Apache Spark. Pull request 51920, closed unmerged. Primary proposal and disposition. The recovery protocol identifies this proposal’s retry-count-100 option as context for the separately gated fixed-profile diagnostic. A closed unmerged PR is not official Spark 3.5.9 tuning guidance, a validated cure or evidence that the profile improves performance or reliability. The fixed recovery configuration and retained actual driver flags determine the study’s scope.
